title: The Bronx to the Desert Chair: Rothbard, the Seminar on Trinity Place, and the State Defined
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Bronx and the Mathematics Degree

stops.name: The Bronx, birth to two immigrants
stops.date_confidence: Date attested (Wikipedia; Mises Institute). Place [R]: no source reached names the family's address. An earlier draft placed the household on the Upper West Side at 40.787, -73.9754; that coordinate is an invention and is discarded. The only locational evidence in Wikipedia is that he attended the public school system 'in the Bronx', and standard accounts have him raised there. The pin is a Bronx-generic point near Bronx Park.
stops.campa: Murray Newton Rothbard is born on the second of March to David Rothbard, a chemist out of Poland, and Rae Rothbard, out of Russia, two Jewish immigrants who have made in one generation the crossing from the Pale to a New York laboratory bench. Among the neighbours is the economist Arthur Burns, a family friend, who thirty years on will sit in judgement on the son's doctorate. The biographies place the household in the Bronx, and it is the Bronx the son will name for the rest of his life whenever he wants a word for what he got out of. The family address is not recovered.
suggested_refs: The 1930 federal census enumeration for the Rothbard household, which would settle the borough

stops.name: The Bronx, the public school he would not forgive
stops.date_confidence: [R] throughout. The sole support is one quoted phrase in Wikipedia, 'the debasing and egalitarian public school system he had attended in the Bronx'. No school is named, no enrolment dates are attested, and the date here orders the segment only.
stops.campa: He is put through the public schools of the borough, and the phrase he uses for them afterwards is fixed and unforgiving: the debasing and egalitarian public school system he had attended in the Bronx. In that phrase the two adjectives are not two complaints. What survives of these years is the grievance, carried whole into a career spent arguing that compulsory schooling is compulsion first and schooling second. No building is named in any source, and no dates of enrolment survive.
suggested_refs: New York City Board of Education enrolment records for the Bronx, 1930s

stops.name: Manhattan, the Birch Wathen School
stops.date_confidence: Attendance [A] (Wikipedia). Location [R] and probably wrong: the pin reconstructs the school's East 71st Street site, but Birch Wathen occupied 9 East 71st Street only from 1962 to 1989, long after he had gone, and this point sits some 400 m from that address in any case. The pre-1962 address is in no reachable source. The name Birch Wathen Lenox is anachronistic here and dates from the 1991 merger.
stops.campa: His parents move him to Birch Wathen, a private school in Manhattan, and he prefers it at once and says so for fifty years. He is not yet fifteen and he already has, in his own person, the comparison the rest of his argument rests on: a thing paid for against a thing compelled. Where the school stood in these years is not in the record. The mansion on East Seventy-first Street that everyone associates with the name is not taken until 1962, and the name itself acquires its second half only in 1991, at a merger he does not live to see.
suggested_refs: Birch Wathen School yearbooks and directories, c. 1938-1942, for the pre-1962 address

stops.name: Columbia University, the mathematics degree
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (Wikipedia; Mises Institute); month set to June by convention for a commencement, not attested.
stops.campa: At nineteen he takes his bachelor's degree from Columbia in mathematics, not in economics. The training holds. For the rest of his life he will build arguments the way a mathematician builds them, from stated premises outward, deducing rather than measuring, and he will treat the econometricians' regressions as a category error rather than as a rival method. Mises has not yet published Human Action in English. Rothbard has not yet heard the word praxeology.
suggested_refs: Columbia University commencement programs, 1945

segments.name: Irvington and the Seminar on Trinity Place

stops.name: Irvington-on-Hudson, the Foundation for Economic Education
stops.date_confidence: [R]. An earlier draft dated this 1946, which is impossible: FEE was founded 7 March 1946 and moved to Irvington later that year, and the FEE article does not state that Rothbard worked there at all. Redated to the late 1940s; the day and month order the segment only. Attested: that Rothbard credited FEE, the institution and not Baldy Harper personally, with creating a 'crucial open center', and that Harper was separately an influence. Coordinate is FEE's Irvington headquarters at 30 South Broadway.
stops.campa: In the years after Columbia he finds his way up the Hudson to Irvington, where Leonard Read has just founded the first free-market outfit of its kind in the country and is running it out of a house above the river. Rothbard vets and edits copy. He credits the Foundation afterwards with having made a crucial open center for a movement that at this date consists of a few hundred people who mostly know each other by post. Baldy Harper, the economist who talent-spots for the cause, notices him here.
suggested_refs: FEE's Irvington-on-Hudson headquarters at 30 South Broadway

stops.name: NYU School of Commerce, the seminar of Ludwig von Mises
stops.date_confidence: Attendance and the 1949 trigger attested (Mises Institute profile); Human Action appeared in September 1949. The building, NYU's Trinity Place commerce campus, is identified from general knowledge and was not independently re-verified.
stops.campa: Human Action appears in September and Rothbard reads it, twenty-three years old, already convinced of the market and not aware there is a whole system standing behind the conviction. He starts attending the unofficial seminar Ludwig von Mises keeps at the NYU business school on Trinity Place, and he will attend it for years and call Mises his teacher for the rest of his life. The room holds graduate students, businessmen and outright cranks. It meets a few streets from the Stock Exchange because no economics department in America will house an Austrian.
suggested_refs: Ludwig von Mises, Human Action (Yale University Press, September 1949)

stops.name: Manhattan, the winter he stops believing in the state
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The Mises Institute profile is the only source for the winter 1949 dating of his turn to individualist anarchism, and no contemporaneous document is cited. The pin is Manhattan-generic: no address is recorded, and this coordinate recurs through the file for that reason.
stops.campa: Some time in the winter he follows the logic one step past his teacher. Mises holds that the market allocates everything except defense and law, which need a state to supply them. Rothbard cannot locate the exception inside the argument. If protection is a service it is a good; if it is a good it is priced; if it is priced it does not require a monopolist with a tax power standing over it. He comes out of that winter an individualist anarchist and stays one for forty-six years. He never persuades Mises of a word of it.
suggested_refs: Rothbard's later account of the 1949 turn in his autobiographical writings

stops.name: Kansas City, the Volker Fund retainer
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'William Volker Fund'); month and day set to January for ordering.
stops.campa: The William Volker Fund of Kansas City, a Missouri lumber fortune turned to the funding of unfashionable scholarship, puts him on retainer as a senior analyst under Baldy Harper's program for finding libertarian talent. His entire living now rests on one foundation continuing to exist. What he gets for it is a salary to read and write on, with no department, no committee, no teaching load and no tenure clock anywhere in it. For a decade the arrangement lets him work like a nineteenth-century man of letters.
suggested_refs: The William Volker Fund papers, Hoover Institution

stops.name: New York City, marriage to JoAnn Schumacher
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (Wikipedia; Mises Institute). Neither month nor venue is recovered; the date defaults to January and the pin is Manhattan-generic.
stops.campa: He marries JoAnn Beatrice Schumacher, a historian. She is not an Austrian economist and does not become one. He calls her the indispensable framework of his life and work. She edits every page he writes for the next forty-two years, which is a very great many pages, and the man who will not concede an inch of theory to anybody hands her the manuscript without argument. The sources give the year of the wedding and nothing else; neither the month nor the room it happened in has been recovered.
suggested_refs: JoAnn Rothbard's editorial hand in the Rothbard papers, Mises Institute

segments.name: The Circle Bastiat and the Break with Rand

stops.name: Murray Hill, Ayn Rand's circle and the first break
stops.date_confidence: Joining in 1954 and the grounds of the departure attested (Wikipedia). An earlier draft placed this in the 1940s, which is wrong by a decade. The coordinate approximates Rand's Murray Hill apartment from general knowledge and was not confirmed.
stops.campa: He is brought into Ayn Rand's circle in her Murray Hill apartment, the collective of admirers reading Atlas Shrugged in manuscript and arguing philosophy until it is light outside. Rothbard does not last. He tells them the system is not new: the ethics come out of Aristotle, the metaphysics out of Aquinas, the politics out of Herbert Spencer, and the author has read all three. There is no room in that apartment for a man who says so. He leaves inside a few months.
suggested_refs: Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, named by Rothbard as the source of Rand's ethics

stops.name: Manhattan, the Circle Bastiat
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia says only 'by the mid-1950s, he helped form the Circle Bastiat'. An earlier draft gave a hard 1954, more precise than any source; the date here orders the segment. No meeting address is recorded, and an earlier draft's coordinate was copied from the discarded Upper West Side birth pin; this is the Manhattan-generic point instead.
stops.campa: By the middle of the decade he has a circle of his own, named for Frederic Bastiat and meeting in apartments around Manhattan: eight or ten young libertarians and anarchists reading Austrian economics and arguing the state out of existence on Saturday nights. They have no institution behind them, no money and no audience, and the vocabulary an entire American movement is still using in 1990 is worked out in those rooms by a dozen people at most. No address for any of them is recorded anywhere, and nobody kept minutes.
suggested_refs: Frederic Bastiat, The Law (1850), the pamphlet the circle took its name from

stops.name: Columbia University, the Panic of 1819
stops.date_confidence: Year, supervisor, subject and Burns's blocking-then-approving all attested (Wikipedia; Mises Institute). Month set to June by convention.
stops.campa: The doctorate comes hard. The dissertation on the Panic of 1819 is written under Joseph Dorfman, and Arthur Burns, the neighbour from the old building and a future chairman of the Federal Reserve, sits in judgement on it and blocks it before finally approving. Eleven years stand between the bachelor's degree and this one. The book that comes out of it stays the standard account of that depression for the rest of the century, a whole American crisis narrated without one appeal to aggregate demand.
suggested_refs: Murray N. Rothbard, The Panic of 1819: Reactions and Policies (Columbia University Press, 1962)

stops.name: Murray Hill, the second and final break
stops.date_confidence: [R] (Wikipedia): that he rejoined after reading Atlas Shrugged and broke a second time over his anarchism. Month and day order the segment. Coordinate as above, unconfirmed.
stops.campa: Atlas Shrugged is published and he reads it and is moved enough to go back. The second stay is shorter than the first. The circle requires that no member hold a position its author has not authorized, and Rothbard by now holds the one position she has called worse than communism, that there should be no government whatever. He leaves for good. Her people will write about the plagiarist for thirty years and he will write about the cult for thirty years, and neither side ever puts it down.
suggested_refs: Ayn Rand, Atlas Shrugged (Random House, 1957)

stops.name: Burlingame, California, the patron dissolves
stops.date_confidence: The Volker Fund's move to Burlingame and its 1962 collapse are attested (Wikipedia, 'William Volker Fund'; Wikipedia, 'Murray Rothbard'). Month and day order the segment. The internal quarrel behind the dissolution is not detailed in anything reached.
stops.campa: The Volker Fund moves its operations to Burlingame on the San Francisco peninsula, and there it comes apart in an internal quarrel and dissolves. Rothbard is thirty-six, with a doctorate, a treatise about to appear, and no salary. The decade of the independent man of letters closes on that news. From here he needs a department, and every department in the country teaches the mathematical economics he has spent fifteen years arguing is not economics. It takes him four years to find one that will have him.
suggested_refs: The William Volker Fund's Burlingame operation and its 1962 dissolution

segments.name: The Treatise, the Pamphlet, and the Wrong Map

stops.name: Princeton, New Jersey, Man, Economy, and State
stops.date_confidence: Publication year and publisher attested (Mises Institute; Wikipedia); D. Van Nostrand was based in Princeton. Month and day order the segment. The Mises endorsement is quoted from the Mises Institute's own page for the combined edition.
stops.campa: Van Nostrand publishes it out of Princeton, two volumes, begun as a study guide to Human Action and grown into a treatise that rebuilds the whole of economics from the single fact that human beings act on purpose. The long section on government intervention is cut by the publisher for length and appears on its own eight years later as Power and Market. Mises, eighty-one and not a man given to praise, reads his student's book and hands him the sentence he carries the rest of his life.
stops.quote: An epochal contribution to the general science of human action, praxeology, and its practically most important and up-to-now best elaborated part, economics.
stops.quote_source: Ludwig von Mises on Man, Economy, and State, quoted on the Mises Institute's page for the combined edition
suggested_refs: Javier Milei's 2023 account of reading Man, Economy, and State, in Pablo Stefanoni, Le Grand Continent, 18 September 2023, cited here as later reception of this book
sources: Mises Institute page for Man, Economy, and State with Power and Market

stops.name: New York City, America's Great Depression
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (Mises Institute profile). Month and day order the segment; the pin is Manhattan-generic, since the book has no place of composition on record.
stops.campa: He publishes the book that puts the Austrian theory of the trade cycle onto the American case: the crash of 1929 and the depression behind it caused not by a market failing but by the credit expansion the Federal Reserve ran through the twenties, and prolonged not by Roosevelt but by Hoover, whom he presents as the first of the interventionists rather than the last of the liquidationists. Nobody in the profession is persuaded in 1963. The book has not been out of print since.
suggested_refs: Murray N. Rothbard, America's Great Depression (D. Van Nostrand, 1963)

stops.name: New York City, What Has Government Done to Our Money?
stops.date_confidence: 1963, Pine Tree Press, per the imprint and the Wikipedia article on the book. The Mises Institute profile gives 1964 and is the outlier; the disagreement is recorded, not resolved. Month orders the segment within the year.
stops.campa: Pine Tree Press issues a small book, under a hundred pages, that explains where money came from, what a gold standard is, what a central bank does to one, and why inflation is a transfer of wealth rather than an accident of weather. It is written for a reader with no economics whatever. Of everything he produces this is the most read, the most translated, and the piece his opponents most often meet first. The Mises Institute's own profile of him misdates it by a year.
suggested_refs: Murray N. Rothbard, What Has Government Done to Our Money? (Pine Tree Press, 1963)
sources: Wikipedia, 'What Has Government Done to Our Money?'

stops.name: New York City, the founding of Left and Right
stops.date_confidence: Founded 1965, ran to 1968, co-founded with George Resch and Leonard P. Liggio (Wikipedia, 'Left and Right: A Journal of Libertarian Thought'). An earlier draft dated the founding to the late 1960s, wrong by several years. Editorial address not recovered; pin Manhattan-generic.
stops.campa: With Leonard Liggio and George Resch he founds a journal on the premise that the political map everyone is using is drawn wrong. Laissez-faire, he argues in the opening essay, was a movement of the left, the party of revolution against kings and guilds and tariffs and standing armies, and the conservatives now claiming it are the heirs of exactly what it fought. It is where the American libertarian movement acquires a history of its own. The journal runs three years and reaches a few hundred readers.
suggested_refs: Murray N. Rothbard, 'Left and Right: The Prospects for Liberty', Left and Right vol. 1 no. 1 (1965)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Left and Right: A Journal of Libertarian Thought'

segments.name: Brooklyn, and the Alliance with the New Left

stops.name: Brooklyn Polytechnic Institute, two days a week
stops.date_confidence: Appointment year and the twenty-year part-time arrangement attested (Wikipedia; Mises Institute). September set for an academic year start, not attested.
stops.campa: An engineering school in Brooklyn hires him to teach economics to undergraduates who are there for the engineering. He comes in two days a week and stays twenty years. There is no graduate program, no doctoral student, no Austrian colleague anywhere in the building, and no prospect of any of the three. He does the real work at home in Manhattan and treats the post as the thing that pays for it. By the account of every student who took the class he is a superb and visibly delighted lecturer.
suggested_refs: Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn course catalogues, 1966-1986

stops.name: New York City, the Peace and Freedom Party and Ramparts
stops.date_confidence: The affiliations are attested (Wikipedia); the geography is loosely attested only. Ramparts was published from San Francisco while Rothbard's own base for this work was New York, so the stop sits at his base and not at the magazine's. Month and day order the segment.
stops.campa: With the war running and the draft taking his students, he goes where the opposition to both actually is. He joins the Peace and Freedom Party, writes for Ramparts, and shares platforms with Students for a Democratic Society, on the argument that conscription is slavery outright and empire is the largest single project the state has. The right he came out of calls this treason. He answers that he has not moved and they have, having traded an old republic for a permanent war economy.
suggested_refs: Rothbard's contributions to Ramparts, 1968

stops.name: New York City, the Libertarian Forum
stops.date_confidence: Founding year, Karl Hess's involvement to 1971, and the 1984 close all attested (Mises Institute; Wikipedia). Month orders the segment. Office address not recovered; pin Manhattan-generic.
stops.campa: He starts a newsletter with Karl Hess, who wrote Barry Goldwater's speeches five years earlier and is now an anarchist working as a welder. It comes out fortnightly, then monthly: eight pages of polemic, running feuds with National Review, book notices, and obituaries written like indictments. Hess leaves in 1971. Rothbard keeps it going alone until 1984, fifteen years of a movement's internal argument conducted by one man with a typewriter and a mailing list.
suggested_refs: The complete run of The Libertarian Forum, 1969-1984

stops.name: New York City, the death wish of the anarcho-communists
stops.date_confidence: The essay and its 1970 date are widely reported but the primary text was not opened this session, so the quote is carried [R] and the month orders the segment. No person is named in the campa because the pool attests none: the pool's links to Bakunin, Lucy Parsons and Rudolf Rocker are thematic word-history inferences, not documents in which Rothbard discusses them.
stops.campa: The alliance with the left breaks on economics. The anarcho-communists who share his hatred of the state do not share his account of how anything at all gets produced without one, and he writes them off in the Forum in an essay whose title is its argument. He is not gentle about it. To will the abolition of the state while willing the abolition of property and of prices is, on his reading, to will a famine and fail to recognize it as one. By the end of the year the alliance is over.
stops.quote: It is no crime to be ignorant of economics, which is, after all, a specialized discipline and one that most people consider to be a 'dismal science.' But it is totally irresponsible to have a loud and vociferous opinion on economic subjects while remaining in this state of ignorance.
stops.quote_source: attributed to Murray N. Rothbard, 'The Death Wish of the Anarcho-Communists' (1970); widely quoted, not verified against the primary text
suggested_refs: Murray N. Rothbard, 'The Death Wish of the Anarcho-Communists', The Libertarian Forum, 1970

stops.name: New York City, For a New Liberty
stops.date_confidence: Publication year attested (Mises Institute profile). Month and day order the segment. The quote is dated to 'Society Without a State' (1975), two years later than this stop, and is carried [R]: widely quoted, primary text not opened.
stops.campa: The manifesto comes out: a whole political order laid out with no state anywhere in it, chapter by chapter through the streets, the courts, the schools, the police, the mails, the poor, and the war. A movement that has been a few hundred people in New York apartments will be, inside the decade, a party on the ballot in fifty states. The book is written to be put into the hands of somebody who has never once heard the argument, and for the next twenty years it is what gets put there.
stops.quote: I define anarchist society as one where there is no legal possibility for coercive aggression against the person or property of any individual.
stops.quote_source: attributed to Murray N. Rothbard, 'Society Without a State' (1975); widely quoted, not verified against the primary text
suggested_refs: Murray N. Rothbard, For a New Liberty: The Libertarian Manifesto (Macmillan, 1973)

stops.name: New York City, the State defined
stops.date_confidence: Anatomy of the State dates from 1974; quotations are verified verbatim against the extracted text of the Mises Institute's 2009 reprint. The gather stage cited this sentence as pp. 11-12; it sits entirely on p. 11, and the citation is corrected. Month and day order the segment; no place of composition is on record and the pin is Manhattan-generic.
stops.campa: He publishes a monograph of about sixty pages that does nothing whatever but define its subject. Not what the state ought to do, not what it does badly, but what it is: an organization marked off from every other organization in society by two facts, that it claims a monopoly of force across a territory and that it takes its income by compulsion instead of by sale. Everything else in the essay is deduced from those two facts. He proposes no remedy in it and does not discuss a single piece of legislation.
stops.quote: Briefly, the State is that organization in society which attempts to maintain a monopoly of the use of force and violence in a given territorial area; in particular, it is the only organization in society that obtains its revenue not by voluntary contribution or payment for services rendered but by coercion.
stops.quote_source: Murray N. Rothbard, Anatomy of the State (Mises Institute, 2009 [1974]), p. 11
suggested_refs: Franz Oppenheimer, Der Staat (1908), source of the phrase 'the political means' that Rothbard builds the definition on
sources: Murray N. Rothbard, Anatomy of the State (Mises Institute, 2009 [1974]), verified from extracted PDF text

stops.name: New York City, the kingdom of South Ruritania
stops.date_confidence: Same book and same verification. Quote verified verbatim at p. 17 of the 2009 Mises edition. The date is an ordering device inside the 1974 publication, not a separate event.
stops.campa: On where states come from he refuses the social contract entirely. Production has to come before predation, since there is nothing to seize until somebody has made it, and therefore the market is older than the state and cannot be its creature. What the record shows, everywhere it shows anything at all, is conquest: a band with weapons takes a district, holds it long enough, and is thereafter addressed as a government by the other governments. He stages the whole process in an invented country, up in the hills, with a bandit chieftain who holds the ground a while and then proclaims himself a king.
stops.quote: In the hills of southern "Ruritania," a bandit group manages to obtain physical control over the territory, and finally the bandit chieftain proclaims himself "King of the sovereign and independent government of South Ruritania"; and, if he and his men have the force to maintain this rule for a while, lo and behold! a new State has joined the "family of nations."
stops.quote_source: Murray N. Rothbard, Anatomy of the State (Mises Institute, 2009 [1974]), p. 17
suggested_refs: Albert Jay Nock, On Doing the Right Thing, and Other Essays (1929), p. 143, quoted approvingly in Rothbard's footnote 5 at p. 16
sources: Murray N. Rothbard, Anatomy of the State (Mises Institute, 2009 [1974]), verified from extracted PDF text

stops.name: New York City, what the intellectuals are paid for
stops.date_confidence: Same book and same verification. Quote verified verbatim at p. 25, where it also stands as the edition's epigraph. A second passage on the manufacture of legitimacy is verified at p. 28; the gather stage cited it as pp. 28-29 and the citation is corrected in the report. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The section that matters most to him is about the people in his own trade. A state cannot hold a territory by force alone, because force is expensive and the population is large; it needs the population to believe it is legitimate, and the manufacture of that belief is contracted out to intellectuals, who are paid in posts, in honours, and in access. He writes this as a man with a two-day-a-week job at an engineering school, refused by the profession for twenty years, describing an arrangement he has watched from just outside it.
stops.quote: The greatest danger to the State is independent intellectual criticism; there is no better way to stifle that criticism than to attack any isolated voice, any raiser of new doubts, as a profane violator of the wisdom of his ancestors.
stops.quote_source: Murray N. Rothbard, Anatomy of the State (Mises Institute, 2009 [1974]), p. 25, also the edition's epigraph
suggested_refs: Anatomy of the State, p. 28, on the State's unremitting effort to distinguish its activities from those of mere brigands
sources: Murray N. Rothbard, Anatomy of the State (Mises Institute, 2009 [1974]), verified from extracted PDF text

stops.name: South Royalton, Vermont, the Austrian revival
stops.date_confidence: [R] on every element including the conference's existence. Two WebFetch attempts on mises.org and a dedicated Wikipedia page all returned 404, and the Austrian School, Israel Kirzner and Institute for Humane Studies articles omit it entirely; it is reported only in secondary Austrian-school histories. An earlier draft's coordinate sat about 1.8 km east of the village and named a 'Royalton College' that no source confirms; the coordinate is corrected to the village itself and no venue is named.
stops.campa: In a Vermont village on the White River a small conference gathers what is left of the Austrian economists of the English-speaking world together with a room of young ones. Rothbard is one of the senior figures who lecture. The tradition has been effectively dead in the American academy since the war, kept breathing in a seminar room on Trinity Place and in a mimeographed newsletter, and this week is where it turns back into a research program with students inside it. Hayek takes the Nobel that autumn.
suggested_refs: Edwin G. Dolan, ed., The Foundations of Modern Austrian Economics (1976), the volume that came out of the conference
sources: Secondary Austrian-school historiography; no primary or encyclopedic source reachable this session

stops.name: New Rochelle, New York, Conceived in Liberty
stops.date_confidence: Volumes I-II 1975, III 1976, IV 1979, from Arlington House of New Rochelle; volume V posthumously from the Mises Institute in 2019 (Wikipedia, 'Conceived in Liberty'). An earlier draft called it a four-volume work; it runs to five. Month and day order the segment.
stops.campa: Arlington House, out of New Rochelle, begins issuing his narrative history of colonial and revolutionary America: two volumes this year, a third the next, a fourth in 1979, told from the standpoint of the settlers, the tax resisters, the rebels against proprietors, and the men who wanted the Revolution carried further than it went. He does not finish it. A fifth volume is assembled out of his manuscripts and published in 2019, twenty-four years after his death.
suggested_refs: Murray N. Rothbard, Conceived in Liberty, 5 vols. (Arlington House 1975-1979; Mises Institute 2019)

stops.name: New York City, the Center for Libertarian Studies
stops.date_confidence: Founding year attested (Mises Institute profile, via Wikipedia summary). Founding address not recovered; pin Manhattan-generic. Month and day order the segment.
stops.campa: He founds an institution, the first of four he will found or co-found in six years, on the recognition that a movement with no money and no buildings stays a mailing list forever. The Center exists to pay for conferences, students, and a journal. Rothbard is fifty. He has spent his entire adult life outside every institution that could have employed him, and he now spends what is left of it building the institutions he was refused. The founding address is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Center for Libertarian Studies founding papers, 1976

segments.name: San Francisco: The Institute He Founded and Was Expelled From

stops.name: San Francisco, the founding of Cato
stops.date_confidence: Founding in January 1977 in San Francisco, with Ed Crane and Charles Koch's funding, attested (Wikipedia, 'Cato Institute'; Wikipedia, 'Murray Rothbard'). The precise founding office address was not recovered; the coordinate is downtown San Francisco.
stops.campa: Ed Crane, Charles Koch, and Rothbard found a think tank in San Francisco and name it for the Cato Letters of the English radical Whigs. Koch supplies the money, Crane supplies the organization, and Rothbard supplies the doctrine and the name. It is the first libertarian institution in America with a serious budget behind it. For four years he sits on the board. For the same four years the question of what exactly the money is for goes unsettled between the three of them.
suggested_refs: John Trenchard and Thomas Gordon, Cato's Letters (1720-1723), the source of the institute's name

stops.name: New York City, the Journal of Libertarian Studies
stops.date_confidence: Founding year attested (Mises Institute profile; Wikipedia). No place is given in any source; the pin is his own Manhattan base and the month orders the segment within the year.
stops.campa: The Journal of Libertarian Studies begins publishing under his editorship, refereed and footnoted and indexed, because he has concluded that a doctrine living only in newsletters will be treated as a hobby for as long as it lives there. Political theory, legal theory, revisionist history, ethics. He is trying to assemble inside one lifetime the apparatus a normal school of thought accumulates across three or four generations. He is fifty-one, and his teaching post is two days a week with undergraduates in Brooklyn.
suggested_refs: The Journal of Libertarian Studies, vol. 1 (1977)

stops.name: Menlo Park, California, the summer conferences
stops.date_confidence: That he was a frequent speaker at Institute for Humane Studies conferences in the 1970s is attested (Wikipedia, 'Institute for Humane Studies'). The IHS address within Menlo Park was not pinned down; the coordinate is downtown Menlo Park. The date orders the segment and does not mark a particular conference.
stops.campa: Baldy Harper's Institute for Humane Studies, working out of Menlo Park on the peninsula, runs summer conferences for students, and Rothbard is on the program year after year. The people sitting in those rooms in the seventies are the people staffing the movement's institutions in the nineties, and a great many of them date their conversion to one week of it. He is short, cheerful and from the Bronx, and he lectures without notes, at speed, laughing at his own material.
suggested_refs: Institute for Humane Studies summer conference programs, Menlo Park, 1970s

stops.name: San Francisco, removed from the board
stops.date_confidence: The removal, the 1980 Ed Clark campaign as its occasion, the split with Edward H. Crane III, and Cato's relocation to Washington the same year are attested (Wikipedia). The stop sits at Cato's outgoing San Francisco base because the move to D.C. is described as following the break. Rothbard's own presence at the vote is not documented in any source checked, and the campa does not stage him in the room. The shares dispute is his own claim and is given as such.
stops.campa: The Libertarian Party's 1980 presidential campaign runs Ed Clark as a low-tax liberal, on Crane's judgement that the full doctrine cannot be sold to anyone. Rothbard says in print that a movement which hides its position has already conceded the argument. In 1981 the board removes him. His shares, he maintains to the end of his life, were taken from him; Crane's people tell it another way, and nobody reconciles the two accounts. The institute moves to Washington that same year.
suggested_refs: The Libertarian Forum's coverage of the Clark campaign and the Cato break, 1980-1981

stops.name: New York City, The Ethics of Liberty
stops.date_confidence: Publication year attested (Mises Institute profile). Month and day order the segment; no place of composition is on record and the pin is Manhattan-generic.
stops.campa: Man, Economy, and State established what a market does. This book establishes what a person may do, and the two together are the whole of the system. He derives the entire content of justice from self-ownership and from original appropriation, applies it without exemption to children, animals, contracts, land titles, and war, and accepts every conclusion the derivation produces, including several that cost him allies he liked. He considers it the most important thing he writes.
suggested_refs: Murray N. Rothbard, The Ethics of Liberty (Humanities Press, 1982)

stops.name: Auburn, Alabama, the Mises Institute
stops.date_confidence: Founding year, Rockwell and Blumert, Rothbard as academic vice president, and the Auburn location are attested (Mises Institute; Wikipedia). Month orders the segment. The Institute operated out of Auburn University rooms until its own building opened across the street in 1998, after his death. No bust, plaque, or physical memorial to Rothbard there is attested in any source checked. The Hoppe quotation is about Man, Economy, and State, not about the Institute.
stops.campa: Llewellyn Rockwell founds an institute in a small Alabama university town, names it for Mises, and makes Rothbard its academic vice president; Burton Blumert helps pay for it. For sixteen years it works out of borrowed rooms on the Auburn campus. It becomes the place where his books are taught, reprinted, digitized, and given away, and where the students who cannot study Austrian economics anywhere else come to study it. Hans-Hermann Hoppe is among the first of that generation.
stops.quote: The book has in the meantime become a modern classic and ranks with Mises's Human Action as one of the two towering achievements of the Austrian School of economics.
stops.quote_source: Hans-Hermann Hoppe on Man, Economy, and State, quoted on the Mises Institute's page for the combined edition
suggested_refs: The Ludwig von Mises Institute's Auburn campus rooms, 1982-1998, before the present building

segments.name: Las Vegas and the Paleo Turn

stops.name: Brooklyn, clearing the office
stops.date_confidence: The departure in 1986 after roughly two decades is attested (Mises Institute; Wikipedia). Month set for an academic year's end, not attested. The tally of books, institutions and journals is arithmetic from attested items.
stops.campa: Twenty years of the two-day week end. He is sixty. He has published nine books, founded or co-founded four institutions, edited three journals, and trained a generation of economists in rented conference rooms, and he has never once held a full-time appointment in an economics department. The Polytechnic gave him undergraduates who wanted engineering credits and a salary that let him write, and it gave him nothing else: no chair, no seminar, no doctoral student. He clears the office and goes west.
suggested_refs: Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn faculty records, 1986

stops.name: University of Nevada, Las Vegas, the S. J. Hall chair
stops.date_confidence: Appointment year, title, and its running until his death are attested (Mises Institute; Wikipedia). September set for an academic year start. Two coordinates for UNLV differing in the fourth decimal were in circulation in the research pool; this file uses one of them throughout.
stops.campa: The University of Nevada makes him S. J. Hall Distinguished Professor of Economics and he moves to Las Vegas at sixty. It is the first endowed chair of his life and he holds it for nine years, which is the rest of his life. After twenty years of undergraduates in Brooklyn who were there for the engineering credits, he has graduate students, a department that actually wants him, and a city built on gambling and legal vice that he sees no reason whatever to apologize for. JoAnn packs the library.
suggested_refs: UNLV Department of Economics faculty records, 1986-1995

stops.name: Auburn, Alabama, the Review of Austrian Economics
stops.date_confidence: Founding in 1987 attested (Mises Institute; Wikipedia). Two separate items in the research pool added that it was 'later renamed the Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics'; that is false and is corrected here. The RAE passed to other editors and then to George Mason University and continues under its own name; the QJAE was established separately by the Mises Institute in 1998.
stops.campa: He founds a second journal, this one for the economics rather than the political theory, and edits it out of the Institute at Auburn. Austrians now have a refereed annual of their own in a discipline that has not made room for them since the 1930s. After his death the journal passes to other editors and eventually to George Mason University, where it continues; the Institute starts a separate quarterly in 1998 to carry the work on in Auburn. The two are constantly mistaken for one.
suggested_refs: The Review of Austrian Economics, vol. 1 (1987)

stops.name: Las Vegas, leaving the Libertarian Party
stops.date_confidence: The 1989 departure from the Libertarian Party and the articulation of the paleolibertarian strategy are attested (Wikipedia). No place is given for either; the stop sits at his own residence and post of the time, and the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: He leaves the Libertarian Party. The Cold War is ending, the anti-interventionist argument no longer has a superpower attached to the other end of it, and he goes looking on the old right for people who will oppose the empire on grounds of their own. The strategy he names paleolibertarian keeps the economics exactly where it was and adds a cultural conservatism the movement's libertines had all assumed was optional. It costs him allies of thirty years' standing. He is sixty-three and does not appear to hesitate.
suggested_refs: Murray N. Rothbard, 'The Case for Paleo-Libertarianism', Liberty, January 1990

stops.name: Auburn, Alabama, the John Randolph Club
stops.date_confidence: Founded 1989 by Thomas Fleming and Rothbard (Wikipedia, 'Paleolibertarianism'); an earlier draft gave 1990, which is the year of the first meeting. No founding venue is recorded anywhere reachable, so the stop sits at the Mises Institute's pin as an ordering device rather than as a claim about where the founding happened.
stops.campa: With Thomas Fleming of the Rockford Institute he founds a club named for the Virginia congressman who opposed nearly everything the nineteenth century proposed to do, and it seats Austrians and paleoconservatives at one table. Where they agree is on the war state, the managerial bureaucracy, and Washington's standing claim to instruct the country in its morals. Where they disagree is on the market, and they never do settle it. The first meeting falls the following year.
suggested_refs: Chronicles, the Rockford Institute magazine edited by Thomas Fleming, for the club's proceedings

stops.name: Atlanta, the Costs of War conference
stops.date_confidence: Talk given at the Mises Institute's Costs of War conference, Atlanta, May 1994, printed as 'Just War' in John V. Denson, ed., The Costs of War: America's Pyrrhic Victories (1997). The quotation is verbatim, verified from the LewRockwell.com text via a 2013 Wayback snapshot. Wikiquote attributes it to 'Two Just Wars: 1776 and 1861', which is the title mises.org gives the audio of the same talk; the printed essay is 'Just War'. Rothbard presents the line inside quotation marks as a slogan, paired with the Irish rebels' motto.
stops.campa: At a Mises Institute conference in Atlanta on the costs of war he argues that only two wars in American history met the conditions of a just one, the Revolution and the Confederate secession, both fought by people defending a territory against an authority claiming it from outside. It is the last full statement of his politics; he has eight months to live. Against the universal rights the century keeps invoking to justify intervention he offers a slogan, and then the motto of the Irish rebels.
stops.quote: Rights may be universal, but their enforcement must be local.
stops.quote_source: Murray N. Rothbard, 'Just War', Costs of War conference, Atlanta, May 1994; printed in John V. Denson, ed., The Costs of War: America's Pyrrhic Victories (Mises Institute / Transaction, 1997)
suggested_refs: John V. Denson, ed., The Costs of War: America's Pyrrhic Victories (1997)
sources: LewRockwell.com text of 'Just War', Wayback snapshot 2013-05-15

stops.name: Manhattan, the heart attack
stops.date_confidence: Date, cause and age attested by two independent fetches (Wikipedia; Mises Institute). The campus is undetermined and the sources contradict: one lens gave the Roosevelt campus at 1000 Tenth Avenue, 40.7714, -73.9878, the other the St. Luke's campus at 1111 Amsterdam Avenue, verified at 40.8056, -73.9617. The two hospitals merged into one center with two campuses in 1978 and no source reached names the building. This file uses the St. Luke's coordinate for both lenses and records the disagreement.
stops.campa: He dies of a heart attack in a Manhattan hospital on the seventh of January, sixty-eight years old, back in the city he never really left. St. Luke's and Roosevelt had merged into a single center with two campuses seventeen years earlier and no source names which of the two buildings it was. Two volumes of a history of economic thought are finished and with the publisher. Lew Rockwell tells the New York Times that Rothbard was the founder of right-wing anarchism.
suggested_refs: The New York Times obituary of Murray Rothbard, January 1995

stops.name: Unionville, Virginia, Oakwood Cemetery
stops.date_confidence: Burial at Oakwood Cemetery, Unionville, Orange County, Virginia is attested via the Wikipedia infobox citing Find a Grave; Find a Grave itself returned HTTP 403 and could not be checked. The day is set to order the segment and is not attested. Three coordinates were in circulation for this grave: 38.1897, -77.9250 and 38.2136, -78.0316, about 10 km apart from each other, and both wrong. Unionville is at 38.2597, -77.9683, which is used here. The plot itself is not located.
stops.campa: He is buried at Oakwood Cemetery in Unionville, Orange County, Virginia, a long way from the Bronx and from Las Vegas both. The plot is not located in any source reachable now, and the coordinates given for the cemetery in different places disagree with each other by miles. William F. Buckley, whom he had fought in print for thirty-five years, publishes an obituary in National Review that declines to be gracious. Hans-Hermann Hoppe calls him an intellectual giant and notes chiefly that, like Mises, he died without the Nobel.
suggested_refs: William F. Buckley Jr.'s obituary of Rothbard, National Review, 1995

stops.name: Las Vegas, the two volumes finished in time
stops.date_confidence: Both volumes of An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought appeared from Edward Elgar in 1995, after his death on 7 January; an earlier draft called only the second posthumous. He completed the two volumes of a longer projected series during his lifetime. The stop sits at the desk where the work was done rather than at the publisher's, and the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: Edward Elgar publishes the two volumes in the year of his death, both of them after it. The first, Economic Thought Before Adam Smith, argues that the Scholastics of Salamanca had subjective value and the entrepreneur four centuries early, and that Adam Smith set the whole discipline backwards by returning to a labour theory of value and writing his own predecessors out of the record. The second follows that error down to Karl Marx and treats him as a millenarian rather than an economist. Three further volumes were planned.
suggested_refs: Murray N. Rothbard, An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought, 2 vols. (Edward Elgar, 1995)
sources: Wikipedia, 'An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought'

stops.name: Auburn, Alabama, the papers and what was left in them
stops.date_confidence: A History of Money and Banking in the United States was published posthumously in 2002 by the Mises Institute from archived manuscripts; the Mises Institute profile's 1999 is wrong by three years. The Logic of Action, two volumes, 1997, rests on the Mises Institute profile alone and is [R]. Spanish editions from 2000 onward are attested in Spanish Wikipedia. Month and day order the segment.
stops.campa: His papers go to Auburn and the Institute publishes what he did not live to publish: The Logic of Action in two volumes, then in 2002 A History of Money and Banking in the United States, assembled out of the manuscripts. He spent his life arguing that ideas travel by circulation and not by credential, and the Institute puts the books on the internet and gives them away. The argument arrives in countries he never visited. Spanish editions follow through the 2000s, one of them into a second edition in 2009.
suggested_refs: The Rothbard Papers, Ludwig von Mises Institute, Auburn
sources: Wikipedia, 'A History of Money and Banking in the United States'
